judgments.reasoning_cat1: The insuring agreement promises payment of death proceeds 'subject to its terms' upon 'due proof' that the insured died while in force; 'due proof' and the open-ended 'subject to its terms' are the kind of phrases parties fight over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read against the Suicide provision (c034) and Incontestability (c033), which cut back the unqualified promise to pay, and against Claims (c030); a beneficiary could argue the face-page promise controls over the internal exclusion.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A 20-day free-look right stated in general terms, with the trigger for the period (delivery? receipt?) obscured, leaves room to argue when the window opens.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits directly against the Right to Return Policy notices (c003-c006), which give 30 or 45 days where the policy replaces an existing policy, so the general 20-day term and the replacement-specific terms point different ways.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is nothing but a heading and an enumerated list of state abbreviations with the operative sentence missing, an archetypal expressio unius/list-scope problem: states not listed get no stated right.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be harmonised with the 20-day cancel right (c002) and the separate replacement-policy windows in c004-c006, and the policy was issued to a Pennsylvania insured governed by c006.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is conditioned on whether 'this life insurance policy replaces an existing policy' — the very term at issue in a replacement dispute — and it enumerates states, inviting an expressio unius reading.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conflicts in duration with the general 20-day cancellation right (c002) and with the CA and PA variants (c005, c006), and the concept of a 'replacement' policy appears nowhere else in the operative text such as the Suicide clause (c034).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The all-caps CA notice turns on the same undefined trigger, whether the policy 'replaces an existing policy', and on an 'unconditional' refund whose scope is not spelled out.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels but differs from c004 and c006 and overrides the 20-day right in c002 for one state only, leaving the state-by-state scheme to be reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Pennsylvania notice is garbled around its condition ('within 45 days of delivery if we issue your ... policy'), so the event starting the 45 days and the condition attaching to it are genuinely unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is the state provision governing this Pennsylvania-issued policy and it cannot be squared with the 20-day right in c002 or the 30-day replacement rights in c004-c005; it is also the only place the instrument acknowledges a replacement context bearing on the suicide clause (c034).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A specifications footnote stating that premiums and charges are affected by risk class and that no one is authorized to represent future changes; it is a simple disclaimer with no contested term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It repeats verbatim at c008 and c014 and is consistent with the Table of Guaranteed Maximum Renewal Premiums and the Premiums provisions, so no internal conflict appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Identical disclaimer language to c007 on the continued specifications page; nothing in it carries two reasonable meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its duplication across pages 3, 3-continued and 6 is consistent rather than conflicting, and it fits the renewal premium table.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A mechanical statement that table installments are monthly and per $1,000 of proceeds; the unit of measure is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It aligns with the option descriptions (c037-c044) and the actuarial basis note (c013) without tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definition of 'age' as age nearest birthday; that is precisely the kind of definitional clause that removes rather than creates ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the life income options basing payments on the payee's age (c037) and with the specification page's issue age.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A parenthetical noting other ages are available on request; it promises only that the company will furnish amounts, a modest and clear statement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates c012 for Option 5 and coheres with the Alternate Life Income clause (c045).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Option 5 parenthetical mirrors c011 and states availability for two males or two females plainly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the Option 5 description (c043) and the general table note (c011) with no discrepancy.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A technical actuarial basis statement (Annuity 2000 table, Scale G, 3% interest); the figures are specific even if the OCR mangles them.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It should be checked against the 4.5% commutation rate in Death of Payee (c046) and the Alternate Life Income rate promise (c045), but the different rates serve different functions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The same risk-class footnote as c007/c008, now on the renewal premium page; a disclaimer of authority with no ambiguous operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with the guaranteed maximum renewal premium table and the Renewal clause (c024) without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause defining when the contract takes effect and how contract months and years run is truncated, and the effective-date trigger (contract date versus issue date) is the sort of term parties dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The specification page shows a contract date of 8/10/07 and an issue date of 8/1/07, while Incontestability (c033) runs from 'date of issue' and the suicide clause (c034) from a different reference point, so measuring the two-year periods depends on reconciling them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A notice takes effect when signed; but it is subject to any payment made or action taken by us before we receive it' sets up a small tension between signing and receipt as the operative moment.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bears on notice-dependent provisions such as Assignment (c027) and Choice of Options (c035), but those expressly require receipt, so the scheme largely coheres.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line definition of 'Option' as payment of proceeds other than in one sum; short but unambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used consistently by Payment of Proceeds (c031) and the Proceeds Payment Options sections (c035-c046).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of payee as the person to whom payments are made and, for life income, the person on whose life the option is based, is definite though the text is clipped.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the option provisions (c036, c040, c043) and the requirement that a death-proceeds payee be the beneficiary (c035).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The pronoun definition makes 'you' mean the insured but the owner 'when referring to contract rights, payments and notices', so which person is addressed shifts by context and is genuinely arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The rider repeats the same definition at c059, and provisions like Proof You Can Be Insured (c020) and the Ownership clause (c026) depend on which meaning applies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The proof must be acceptable to us' is a discretionary standard whose boundary a court could be asked to fix.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works together with Reinstatement (c025) and Conversion (c047), which excuses proof of insurability, so its reach interacts with those but does not plainly contradict them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The risk class definition survives only as a fragment ('Unless we adopt other rules, your risk...'), leaving the classification standard unstated and reserving unilateral rule-making.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Risk class drives premiums under the specification footnotes (c007, c014) and the conversion premium clause (c051), so an undefined class ripples through those.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The payment clause fragment ('Premiums after the first one ... in advance of the period to which they apply') states a plain advance-payment rule.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with the Grace Period (c023) and Renewal (c024) provisions and with the premium tables on pages 3 and 6.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grace period clause is unusually complete and specific: 31 days, termination retroactive to the due date, notice, and deduction of due premium from death proceeds.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The retroactive termination 'as of the premium due date' sits slightly oddly with paying death proceeds for a death during grace, but the clause itself resolves that by subtraction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Renewal by paying 'the premium then due' with no renewal past 'the final term date shown on page 3' is definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Page 3 of this policy shows years payable and a premium guarantee period while the renewal dates run on page 6 to 2049, so the cross-reference to a final term date on page 3 may not match the document.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reinstatement conditions are enumerated (application, approval, past due premiums with interest) but the text breaks off, leaving the time limit and interest terms unstated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Reinstatement restarts the contestable period under Incontestability (c033) and potentially the suicide period (c034), so its interaction with those two-year clocks is a live issue.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ownership fragment refers to naming a revocable beneficiary or contingent owner; too little survives to identify a contested term but nothing is obviously two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to the Beneficiary and Proceeds Payment Option sections (c028, c035), which are consistent with owner control while the insured lives.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The assignment fragment says the company is not bound unless it receives notice and that the assignee's claim is prior; standard and definite in substance.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Notice (c016) and Beneficiary (c028) on priority of claims, with no visible contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The beneficiary clause is clipped precisely where it says what happens if no beneficiary survives, and class-share language ('the rights of a person ... the same class') is the kind of wording estates litigate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be read with the insuring agreement's promise to pay the beneficiary (c001) and with the option rule that a death-proceeds payee must be the beneficiary (c035).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Statements are 'true as far as you know and believe' yet not warranted if made in good faith, and denial requires the statement be in an attached application — layered qualifications that invite argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the pivot between the application and Incontestability (c033), and in a replacement-policy dispute the accuracy of application statements about the replaced policy is exactly where the two provisions meet.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Payment 'within 30 days after we receive proof of the death of the insured' is a definite deadline tied to a definite trigger.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with the due-proof requirement in the insuring agreement (c001) and the interest provision (c032), though the suicide clause (c034) may defer payment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the fragment 'in one sum unless an option is chosen. We may ...' survives; the default lump-sum rule is clear but the reserved discretion is missing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the Option definition (c017) and Choice of Options (c035).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Interest 'at the rate of at least X% per year, but not less than that required by law' leaves the floor to external law and the running period is garbled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with Claims (c030) on the 30-day payment window and with option interest under Option 1 (c038), without a plain contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The incontestability text turns on '2 years after date of issue or 2 years after any reinstatement' with a carve-out for non-payment of premiums; the measuring date and what counts as a contest are classic construction battlegrounds.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be squared with the Suicide clause (c034), which is a separate two-year bar, with the contract/issue date discrepancy in c015 and the specifications, and with the conversion incontestability clause (c055) — a replacement policy makes the start date genuinely contested.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The suicide exclusion is fragmentary but its operative terms — 'suicide or intentional self-destruction' 'while insane', a period 'in effect for less than 2 years', and the refund-of-premiums remedy — are exactly the phrases suicide-clause litigation turns on.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: In a policy that elsewhere acknowledges replacing an existing policy (c004-c006) and that has separate incontestability (c033), contract-date/issue-date (c015) and conversion suicide (c055) provisions, whether the two years runs from this contract or the replaced one cannot be settled from the clause alone.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rule that the owner may choose an option while the insured lives and that a death-proceeds payee must be the beneficiary is stated definitely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits Beneficiary (c028), Ownership (c026) and the corporate payee clause (c036), which allows other payees only by agreement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Anyone else related to the insured by blood or marriage' after a list of specific relations is a general catch-all against enumerated specifics, though the company's consent gates it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It qualifies the general choice-of-options rule in c035 and is expressly permissive, so the two read together coherently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The description-of-options preamble (endorsement to show option terms; other arrangements 'if you request and we approve'; life income based on payee's sex and age) is administrative and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the settlement tables (c009-c013) and the individual option provisions that follow.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Option 1 fragment states a guaranteed interest rate with discretion to announce a higher one and interest payable at stated frequencies; discretionary excess interest is common and bounded.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the death proceeds interest clause (c032) and the Death of Payee rule that for option 1 the amount due is any balance held (c046).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Almost nothing survives beyond a right to withdraw the proceeds; no identifiable ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It aligns with the option 2 table on page 4 and the commuted-value rule for option 2 in c046.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The life income fragment states the first payment is due on the option date and payments continue while the payee lives; plain in substance.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reads consistently with the option 3 tables, the installment refund variant (c041) and the alternate life income clause (c045).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The installment refund mechanic — level payments until the sum equals the proceeds applied, then continuing for life — is arithmetically definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with the option 3 table columns and with the commutation rule for option 3 in c046.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Option 4's fragment (final payment equals the unpaid balance; right to withdraw) is a standard and clear mechanic.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches c046's rule that for option 4 the amount then due is any balance held by us.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The joint and survivor description ('These options are for 2 payees') is definite so far as it goes, with the payment level fixed by the page 5 table.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the option 5 table note (c012) and the joint-and-two-thirds variant (c044).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The joint and 2/3 mechanic — full payment while both live, a reduced payment after the first death — is stated clearly though the fraction wording is OCR-damaged.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with c043 and the option 5 tables; nothing else in the instrument speaks to survivor reduction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Rates at least as liberal as those we charge as of the option date for a single premium immediate annuity of the same kind' uses the vague comparator 'at least as liberal' and the undefined 'of the same kind'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with the guaranteed table basis (c013) and with c046's statement that the commutation rate will be specified when an alternate life income is chosen, which leaves the default 4.5% rate's application uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause fixes a 4.5% commutation rate for options 2, 3 and 5 and balance-held treatment for 1 and 4, then says the commutation rate will be separately specified for alternate life incomes — two rules for one variable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That carve-out points back to Alternate Life Income (c045) and sits against the 3% table basis in c013, so the applicable rate depends on reading several provisions together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The conversion preamble survives only as 'may be converted to a new contract ... you will not have to prove that you can be insured'; the waiver of insurability proof is clear but the conditions are missing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is qualified by the conversion date, plan, amount, premium, notice, rider and disability clauses (c048-c054) and by Proof You Can Be Insured (c020), which it displaces.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The conversion date fragment ties the new contract's effect to the later of the conversion date and payment of premium; definite in structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the notice requirement (c052) requiring a request within 31 days before the conversion date, and no conflict is apparent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The new contract may be any whole life plan that we [then issue]' reserves the plan menu to the insurer; a common but not ambiguous formulation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the amount and premium clauses (c050, c051) and the disability conversion clause (c054).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The amount rule ('not more than the converted part of this contract' and at least our minimum whole life issue limit) sets both a ceiling and a floor by reference to an internal underwriting limit that is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The same undefined minimum issue limit appears in the disability conversion clause (c054) and in the rider qualifying requirements (c062), so the term is used but never fixed anywhere in the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The premium for the converted contract is set at 'our then published rates' for the plan and the insured's age, with a garbled sentence about the risk class carrying over; the risk-class carry-over is the arguable part.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the undefined Risk Class provision (c021) and on the specification footnotes (c007, c014) disclaiming any representation about future risk-class change.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The requirement to ask for the new contract 'within 31 days before the conversion date' with the insured alive on both dates is a definite, if awkwardly phrased, deadline.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It pairs with the conversion date clause (c048) and the last-day-to-convert references in c053 and c054 without visible contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The riders clause piles up specific prohibitions (waiver of premium, accidental death, issue-age limits, greater accidental death amount) and closes with the open catch-all 'You may only have other riders if we agree', a general-versus-specific structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with the Accelerated Benefit Rider attached to this policy (c056-c073) and with the disability conversion clause (c054), which permits conversion when premiums are being waived, so the exclusions and the exception must be reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disability conversion fragment refers to premiums being waived, conversion to a whole life plan chosen by us, and the minimum issue limit, all under 'the rider's terms' — conditions that are stated only obliquely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-references a waiver of premium rider not attached to this policy and cuts against c053's prohibition on carrying a waiver rider into the new contract.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the word 'contract' survives of a heading 'Incontestability and Suicide', so the provision's operative content — whether the periods run from the original or the new contract — is unstated on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Whatever it says must be squared with Incontestability (c033) and the Suicide clause (c034), and the question of a successor contract inheriting or restarting those periods is the same question a replacement policy raises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reduction rule says death proceeds will be reduced and the premium reduced to the level 'appropriate for the reduced death proceeds', with the formula deferred to Contract Values; 'appropriate' is doing real work.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the premium reduction statement at c072 and points to the Contract Values formula at c070, so the amount of reduction can only be derived by combining three provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surviving text is only 'contract differ, the rider controls', a bare priority rule whose scope (which differences, which contract terms) is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly a conflict-resolution clause, so it engages every place the rider and policy overlap — the pronoun definitions (c019 vs c059), payment options (c069 vs c035) and premium reduction (c056, c072).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The effective date rule ('the later of the contract effect[ive date] ...') is truncated, leaving the second alternative unstated, but the 'later of' structure is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It should be read with the contract months and years clause (c015) and the specification page's differing contract and issue dates, which is where a start-date dispute would arise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rider's pronoun definition again makes 'you' the insured except that it means the owner for contract rights, a context-dependent split that can be read two ways.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates c019 in the policy's general definitions, and given the rider-controls clause (c057) any divergence in wording between the two would have to be resolved.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Practitioner of the medical arts licensed in the United States' who is not a family member or household member is reasonably precise, though 'medical arts' has some soft edges.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used consistently by the qualifying requirements (c062), terminal condition (c063) and medical referee (c067) provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The benefits fragment ('payment to the owner of a[n accelerated amount] ... condition ... if you have more than one contract with us') is missing its amount limits and aggregation rule.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The maximum benefit and any aggregate cap belong with Contract Values (c070) and the qualifying requirements (c062), so its scope is only knowable from those.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The qualifying requirements are an enumerated list whose items are partly garbled, including a condition that other persons with rights in the contract 'cannot change' and an undefined 'minimum issue limit we allow for contracts like this'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The minimum issue limit also appears in the conversion amount clause (c050) without definition, and consent of assignees and beneficiaries ties back to c027 and c028.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Terminal condition' — a non-correctable condition that will 'with reasonable medical certainty' result in death within a stated period — turns on a medical-certainty standard that is the archetype of a litigated definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It anchors the qualifying requirements (c062), request for payment (c064) and the medical referee dispute mechanism (c067), which itself presupposes physicians can disagree about it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of a 'request for payment' as the owner's written request accompanied by proof of terminal condition is procedural and definite, though clipped.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the qualifying requirements (c062) and the additional-proof clause (c065) with no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Reserving the right to require additional proof and an examination by a physician of the insurer's choice at its expense is a clear allocation, though 'additional proof' is open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leads directly into the medical referee clause (c067) and the cost-allocation clause (c068), which together form a coherent process.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A recommendation to consult a tax advisor before adding the rider or requesting payment; hortatory, not operative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the instrument depends on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The referee mechanism is detailed — a disinterested third physician 'acceptable to both' whose decision the insurer will accept — but 'acceptable to both' leaves no tiebreaker if the physicians cannot agree.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It builds on the physician definition (c060) and the additional-examination right (c065), and its cost consequences are set out in c068.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cost split (we pay our physician and the referee, you pay your physician's time) is a plain allocation despite the OCR damage.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It dovetails with the referee clause (c067), which promises an additional payment if the decision is in the insured's favor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Payment in a lump sum or, at the owner's choice, under any proceeds payment option 'except those which are contingent on the life of the insured' — the exception requires classifying each of options 1 to 5.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That exception must be applied against Options 3 and 5 (c040, c043), which are life-contingent, and against the rule in c035 that a death-proceeds payee be the beneficiary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Contract Values formula survives only as 'A is the benefit paid under this rider ... $100 ... state where this rider is issued', so the reduction calculation itself is not legible in the provision.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the referenced source for the reductions promised in c056 and c072 and for the interest rate in c071, so those provisions cannot be applied without it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The interest ceiling is defined with unusual precision by reference to Moody's Composite Yield on Seasoned Corporate Bonds and a stated fallback, which narrows rather than widens the room to argue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The fallback to an average 'acceptable to the state insurance commissioner' fits the state-of-issue reference in c070; no conflict appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Premiums will reduce to the level required for the reduced amount of the death proceeds' is a mechanical rule, marred only by a doubled verb in the OCR.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It repeats c056's premium reduction sentence in slightly different words ('appropriate for' versus 'required for'), and given the rider-controls clause (c057) the duplication invites a comparison.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A termination clause listing the earliest of several events, of which only two survive; a truncated enumeration whose remaining triggers are unstated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It ties to the contract's own termination on non-payment (c023) and to the exhaustion of the benefit under c070, and nothing contradicts it.
